periods.label: August 1958

levels.sentence: With the first American printing of Lolita already gone from the bookshops, I walk out to find the bright cover in a window beside a can of soup, return to Véra's typed reply and the small knell of the telephone, and at dinner raise a glass to the child who is not a child and to the language that held her up — without illusions about the scandal, yet pleased that the world has sat up.
levels.paragraph: The first American printing is already disappearing from the shelves, and I walk out to watch the bright cover in a window, next to a can of soup. I feel a quiet pride, as if I had smuggled a tropical butterfly into a snowstorm. Véra has typed a reply to our first fan letter; the telephone rings like a small knell. At dinner we drink a glass of wine to the child who is not a child, and to the language that held her up. I have no illusions about the scandal, yet there is deep pleasure in having made the world sit up.
levels.summary:
My publishers tell me the first American printing is disappearing, so I go out to see the little book in its new flesh. There it is, propped in a shopwindow beside a can of soup, and the sight fills me with a strange pride — as if I had smuggled a tropical butterfly into a snowstorm.

At home Véra has already answered the first fan letter, and the telephone rings now and then like a small knell, tolling the beginning of something.

In the evening we drink a glass of wine to the child who is not a child, and to the language that held her up through all the years of her long flight. I am not deceived about the scandal to come; one can smell it in the air. But there is deep pleasure in having made the world sit up.

The butterfly is out, and no storm can quite claim it back.

periods.label: October 1961

levels.sentence: On the first of October, 1961, we have taken high rooms at the Montreux-Palace above the lake, and in the pale lavender light I recognize the exact color of a memory about to be written — and know I shall end my days here, without terror.
levels.paragraph: Today we have moved into the Montreux-Palace, high above water whose name I can pronounce only with a French smile. The rooms are damasked and full of light, and the manager has already asked if I am a writer. My index-card drawer sits on the desk, Véra has hung a small Russian icon above the bed, and the Alpine light is that pale lavender tint of a memory on the point of being written. I believe I shall finish my life here, and the thought no longer frightens me.
levels.summary:
On the first of October, 1961, we settled into the Montreux-Palace, high above the lake with its unpronounceable name. The rooms are generous, with damask and a wide view of the water; the manager asked at once whether I was a writer, and I felt the odd courtesy of being recognized in that way.

The movers placed my index-card drawer on the desk, and Véra hung a small icon above the bed, so that the room already begins to feel inhabited.

The light here is the light of the high Alps — pale, lavender, tender — exactly the color of a memory that has not yet been written down. I looked at the water and the mountains and found that the idea of ending my days in this place no longer seemed terrible, but rather something like the closing of a well-made book.

The drawers are full of notes; the icon watches; the lake below keeps its steady pulse. I think I can work here.

periods.label: June 1977

levels.sentence: As my body slows, the mind keeps its steady hum, and the index cards of Laura begin to speak in a new voice, while outside the lake lies like dark mother-of-pearl and Véra brings tea through the scent of balcony roses, reminding me that the one shadow I have chased all my life is the one I will never catch.
levels.paragraph: The body's engine idles down, yet the mind still hums all night, much like that fluorescent light in a collecting hut. I shuffle the index cards of Laura, and they start to murmur to one another — a voice I had not heard before. The lake is a dark sheet of mother-of-pearl; I half-see a white butterfly drifting over the water, a memory or a wish. Véra comes with tea and speaks of the roses blooming on the balcony. I have spent a lifetime running after shadows; the last one, of course, will not be caught.
levels.summary:
On this last evening of June, I feel the body's motor slowing, but the mind keeps its nocturnal murmur — like the fluorescent tube in some long-ago collecting hut. I have been arranging the index cards of Laura, and little by little they have begun to speak to one another in a voice I have never quite heard.

Outside, the lake lies dark as mother-of-pearl, and in the glass of memory I fancy a white butterfly drifting over the water.

Véra enters with a cup of tea and tells me the balcony roses are in bloom; her presence is as certain as the gathering dusk. I have spent my whole life chasing shadows — of wings, of words, of lost time. This last shadow, I know, is the one I shall not catch. That knowledge settles softly, like tea-light on a table.

periods.label: Family

I hear my mother's hidden-flute laughter, and see her lifting a dusty butterfly with the reverence of a prayer. levels.summary:
Of my father, the clearest image is the lamplight on his monocle as he read, and the sudden flap of a newspaper when an argument took hold. He taught me to ride a bicycle on the frozen Nevka; the black ice sang under the tires, and his hand was a steady pressure against my shoulder.

His pride in our name was not a boast but a quiet certainty, a bright thing without wings, which I have carried ever since.

My mother, Elena Ivanovna, woke me on the first morning of 1899 with a whisper; I remember less the sound than the warmth. Her laughter seemed to come from a hidden flute behind her collarbone, and I would lean toward it as toward a light.

She kept my earliest verses in a small box beside her pearls, and after we left Russia that box followed us from room to borrowed room, a modest treasury we opened only with ceremony.

Her tenderness for my butterfly specimens puzzled me then; she would take a dusty wing between her fingers and look at it as others admire a hymn. I thought it was kindness. Now I see she was teaching me that nothing need be beautiful to become sacred—only remembered.

On New Year's Day, 1925, the Berlin winter lay grey against the panes while Véra typed my words faster than I could speak them. Dmitri, then a child, wandered in humming, his voice already deep with the echo of shipboard songs from our exile.

When I read aloud from a rough novel and came to a line that made me swallow a laugh, Véra, without a word, reached across and marked the exact spot with a tiny pencil stroke; Dmitri laughed outright.

That was our way: we were a lighthouse to one another, each a beam for the other two, braided into a small helix of light that kept the Berlin darkness at bay.

periods.label: Places

levels.sentence: Vyra taught me the grammar of place, Berlin forgave me by ignoring me, and America, with a quiet shift at five thousand feet, released my Russian bones into its light.
levels.paragraph: I have claimed three landscapes in my life, and each claimed me in turn. Vyra was a page I knew by heart, its birches and mint-green lawn writing themselves into me before I had words. Berlin, with its weeping gas-ring and yellow wallpaper, never asked for my loyalty, and in that negligence I found a strange pardon. America entered through the eyes and pores, until at last my old bones gave way to its light and I belonged.
levels.summary:
Vyra was my entire world, the only geography I have ever cared to claim. I recall the high birches, the lawn descending in a sheet of cool mint to the Oredezh, and the greenhouse smelling of wet clay and geraniums.

As a child I walked every footpath until it knew me as well as I knew it, reading my own history in the dust. Later I understood that Vyra was not scenery but a language — the grammar of my mind.

Berlin asked nothing of me. I wrote my first Sirin novels at a wobbly table in a pension whose yellow wallpaper had seen better days, while trams shook the window-glass like a held breath.

In the Tiergarten, beneath the Siegessäule, I went hunting for a cabbage butterfly and was simply a naturalist with a net for a while. The city forgave my solitude without noticing it, and that was enough.

America I crossed in a car that smelled of gasoline and old maps, a butterfly net tied to the roof-rack like a fragile antenna. The horizons unrolled their watercolors — pinkish mesas, violet gullies, long pale skies — and in the mountain meadows the sage gave off a dry perfume.

At five thousand feet I stood still and felt a quiet shift: my Russian bones, formed by cold and caution, gave way to the American light. It was not a surrender but a release, and from that hour I knew I could belong.

periods.label: Butterflies

levels.sentence: I learned to read butterflies — by the quiver of their flight, the tiles of their scales, the violet edge of a pinned wing — and in that reading I found an exactness of place and love that exile could never erase.
levels.paragraph: From the first muslin net the village carpenter bent for me, I learned to tell male from female by the shade of a butterfly's flight — a kind of reading in the air. My first pinned Camberwell Beauty, on a September afternoon, opened a cork-lined room I have never left, with its hush of pin and camphor. At Harvard, sorting Polyommatus scales under the microscope, my left eye gazed at those minuscule tiles while my right kept watch for a red admiral at the window; that double vision brought me as near as I ever came to marrying exact science to pure ecstasy. And on the Western trips, guided by black peaks and flowers, I gathered not only Speyeria but the precise yellow of a sulphur and Véra's chortle from the car — a homeland that travels with me still, green and exact.
levels.summary:
From the village carpenter's muslin net I learned a delicate art: to smell the difference between a male and a female butterfly by the very shade of its flight.

That quivering shadow was a text more legible than any book, and my first pinned Camberwell Beauty — its violet-edged wing a map of paradise — opened a cork-lined room whose camphor scent and wooden hush I still carry.

During the Harvard years I sorted Polyommatus in the Museum of Comparative Zoology, my first salaried work. It was nothing but looking at wing scales, those tiny blue and violet tiles that shifted in the light, and I would have done it for nothing.

While my left eye stayed at the microscope, my right kept a separate watch for a red admiral passing the window; the two ways of seeing — the contemplative and the expectant — made a strange harmony, and in that balance I came nearest to marrying exact science to pure ecstasy.

On our Western trips we searched the high Colorado meadows for Speyeria, guided by the black peak and by the flowers they favored. I had their names in three languages, a small vanity; the true mementos were visual and acoustic — the precise yellow of a male sulphur under a blue sky, and Véra's chortle from the car.

That knowledge of place, of light, of her voice settled in me so firmly that exile could not undo it. Those trips gave me a homeland that travels with me, still green, still exact.

periods.label: Writing

levels.sentence: In the Sirin years I posted painted eggshells to a lost Russia, then lived seven years inside Lolita's beautiful disease, and at last tried to rub away the stain of time in Speak, Memory — each labor a way of recovering the shadow I had misplaced somewhere along the way.
levels.paragraph: Under the mask of Sirin I wrote to keep a vanished country alive, each book a careful letter in an eggshell. Years later, Lolita pursued me like a beautiful disease until I set it down on index cards in motel light. Then came Speak, Memory, my attempt to prove that time is not a wall but a stain, and that loving attention might rub it away. Standing on the same grass as my child self, I tried to let the past return to me — not by going back, but by waiting for the creak of a stair, the weight of a shadow.
levels.summary:
During the Sirin years I wrote under a pseudonym, as if the name itself could bear the weight of a lost country. Mashenka, The Defense, The Gift — each was a brittle, painted eggshell posted to a Russia I could no longer touch.

I filled them with remembered colors and corners, believing that precise description might conjure it back. The Gift ended with a chapter that was one long sentence bending into a question mark, written in a single evening of snow-light.

When I set the pen down, I felt I had misplaced my own shadow — not grief, but a quiet, amused bewilderment, like mislaying a favorite glove.

I set down Lolita on index cards, in stolen hours beside a sleeping wife in the front seat of a car, on motel porches, in the rural silence of Ithaca. The origin was a newspaper article about an ape that, having learned to draw, rendered the bars of his cage.

That image stayed with me, and for seven years the novel pursued me like a beautiful disease. It broke my heart on many pages, but the ache was worth it. The writing was a kind of captivity — my own cage of obsession — from which I could emerge only by setting down the words.

Even now, the memory of that labor carries a strange tenderness, like looking back at a fever.

In Speak, Memory I wanted to prove that time was a stain, not a wall, and that a sufficiently loving attention could rub it away. I stood on the same grass where I had stood as a child, placing my foot exactly where my smaller self had left its pressure, trying to make the years jump.

The trick was not to return to the past but to let it return to me—through the creak of a stair, the smell of a lamp, the exact weight of a shadow in the nursery. The book grew from that attempt; it is not a chronicle but a maze, with a corridor and a glimmer and a thread leading back to the nursery.

I wrote it because I believed that if I rubbed hard enough at time's stained surface, the bright grain would show, and the child I had been might step out of the grass to meet me.

periods.label: Teaching

levels.sentence: At Cornell I faced hungry first-year faces, called great literature a fairy tale turned inside out, and afterward spent twelve years translating Pushkin's Onegin until, with the proofs done, I wept at the sudden knowledge that my companion was gone.
levels.paragraph: I remember the hundred sharp young faces at Cornell and the faint blue ticks I left in their margins, patient as larvae. Then came the long years inside Onegin, tracking every iamb and rhyme, writing a commentary that was really a love-letter. When the last proofs arrived, I wept, not from relief, but from the silence that followed. The book is done; my friend is gone again; the pages hold the vigil.
levels.summary:
At Cornell I faced a hundred first-year faces, each hungry for certainty, and told them that great literature is a fairy tale turned inside out. They took the words down without a smile, as if they were specimens, and I marked their papers with small blue ticks — faint, exact, like butterfly eggs.

I liked the quiet hope in those ticks, patient as larvae, waiting for warmth to become what they already were.

Then for twelve years I lived inside Pushkin's Onegin, falling after every iamb and stumbling over every rhyme. The commentary became a love-letter, and the work restored my Russian, which exile had worn thin.

When the last proofs came, I found myself weeping — not from relief, but from the sudden knowledge that a dear companion had been absent all along. There is a peculiar solitude in spending so long with one voice, and the finished book left a silence that felt immense.

The pages remain, filled with that long vigil. I had kept him near by translating him, and now that it stood finished, I had to learn to let the silence be. My friend is gone again, but the work is there, breathing on the shelf.

At Cornell I faced a hundred first-year faces, each hungry for certainty, and told them that great literature is a fairy tale turned inside out. They took the words down without a smile, as if they were specimens, and I marked their papers with small blue ticks — faint, exact, like butterfly eggs.

I liked the quiet hope in those ticks, patient as larvae, waiting for warmth to become what they already were.

Then for twelve years I lived inside Pushkin's Onegin, falling after every iamb and stumbling over every rhyme. The commentary became a love-letter, and the work restored my Russian, which exile had worn thin.

When the last proofs came, I found myself weeping — not from relief, but from the sudden knowledge that a dear companion had been absent all along. There is a peculiar solitude in spending so long with one voice, and the finished book left a silence that felt immense.

The pages remain, filled with that long vigil. I had kept him near by translating him, and now that it stood finished, I had to learn to let the silence be. My friend is gone again, but the work is there, breathing on the shelf.

levels.sentence: On the first morning of 1961, I watched the gray lake from the Palace in Montreux, wrote until noon, walked with Véra and the dog, and, sorting the cards of The Original of Laura, found contentment in the paradise of fragments rather than in an ending.
levels.paragraph: From the Palace window on the first morning of 1961, the lake lay gray as abalone, and the mountains kept their snow like a secret. I breakfasted at nine, wrote until noon, then walked with Véra and the dog by the cold water, savoring the thin brightness of the air. Later the mirror returned an old man with a Nabokov face, eyes lined, but the mind still hummed at the altitude of the Russian novels. Sorting the index cards of The Original of Laura, I felt a new character stir — a third woman with a sweet little face — and the cedar scent of the cards, the broken brass butterfly pin, held the moment fast. I knew the novel would stay unfinished, yet arranging the cards gave me a self-contained joy: the paradise of the work lies in its fragments, not its ending.
levels.summary:
On the first day of 1961 in Montreux, I woke to a lake gray as abalone and mountains holding their snow like a secret. After breakfast I wrote until noon, then walked with Véra and our dog beside the cold water, the air thin and bright with the high season.

In the mirror I met an old man with a Nabokov face, his eyes lined, but the mind unchanged, still humming at the altitude of the Russian novels.

Later I sorted the index cards of The Original of Laura and felt the early thrill of a new character — a third woman with a sweet little face — taking shape. The cedar scent and the broken brass butterfly pin beside the cards anchored the moment in memory.

I knew the novel would remain unfinished, but the arranging gave me a quiet, self-contained joy; the paradise of the work lies in its fragments, not in its ending. I was content.

levels.sentence: From my father's lamplight and monocle, from the black ice of the Nevka, from my mother's whispered warmth and the mint-green grammar of Vyra, I learned that home is not a place left behind but an inheritance carried in the mind.
levels.paragraph: My father taught me in lamplight, his monocle glinting as he read or snapped a newspaper, and his hand on my bicycle was steady enough to keep the frozen Nevka from taking me. My mother's first whisper of 1899 was a warmth I remember better than its sound, and her quiet reverence for my dusty butterfly specimens was a lesson in the sacraments of memory. Vyra itself was the true language: birches, mint lawn, the greenhouse smelling of wet clay and geraniums, and footpaths I knew as one knows a page.
levels.summary:
Father emerges for me always in lamplight, the steel rim of his monocle catching the glow as he read to us, or in the sharp flap of a newspaper when an argument took him.

That winter, on the frozen Nevka, he kept his steady hand on my bicycle and let the black ice sing under the tires; I can still hear the sound, and I can still feel the pride in our name as a bright, unwinged certainty I carried everywhere.

My mother, Elena Ivanovna, woke me on the first morning of 1899 with a whisper, and what I remember is less the sound than the warmth. Her laughter lived somewhere behind her collarbone, a hidden flute I leaned toward as toward a light.

She kept my earliest verses in a small box beside her pearls, and after we left Russia that modest treasury followed us through every borrowed room, opened only with ceremony.

When she took a dusty butterfly between her fingers and looked at it as others look at a hymn, I thought it was kindness; now I see she was teaching me that a thing need not be beautiful to be sacred, only remembered.

Vyra was my entire world, the only geography I would ever care to claim: high birches, a lawn descending in cool mint to the Oredezh, a greenhouse that smelled of wet clay and geraniums. I walked every footpath until I knew it as one knows a page, reading in the dust my own repeated history.

Only now, from a distance, do I understand that Vyra was not merely a place but a language, and no other setting has ever asked such loyalty of me.

levels.sentence: The village carpenter made me my First net of muslin and bent cane, and in its gentle arc I discovered the whole secret economy of butterfly flight — a Camberwell Beauty's violet-edged wing that has kept me, ever since, in a cork-lined room.
levels.paragraph: The village carpenter made me a First net of muslin around a bent cane, and I learned to tell the scent of male from female in the shade of their passing. One September afternoon I pinned my first Camberwell Beauty, its violet-edged wing a small map of paradise. I have never really left that cork-lined room; the grain of the cork and the faint tang of camphor are the fixed points of my memory.
levels.summary:
The village carpenter made me a First net of muslin stretched over a bent cane, and with it I learned a delicate art: to smell the difference between male and female butterflies by the shade of their flight. That quivering shadow of color taught me more than any book could, a kind of reading in the air.

My first pinned specimen was a Camberwell Beauty on a September afternoon, its violet-edged wing a map of paradise.

That moment opened a cork-lined room I have never really left; the scent of camphor and the feel of the cork still bring back the exact hush of the pin going in, and the wing settling into its new, eternal stillness.

levels.sentence: Berlin treated me well enough, letting me write my Sirin novels at a shaky table and hunt a cabbage butterfly in the Tiergarten, and then, without a word, forgiving me my solitude.
levels.paragraph: We lived in pension rooms with yellow wallpaper and a gas-ring that wept with us, yet Berlin was not unkind. I wrote my first Sirin novels at a shaky table while the trams made the window-glass tremble like a held breath. In the Tiergarten I looked for a cabbage butterfly in the shadow of the Siegessäule. The city forgave me my solitude, and that was its only verdict.
levels.summary:
We lived in pension rooms whose yellow wallpaper had seen better days, and a gas-ring that seemed to weep with us. Yet Berlin itself was lenient. At a wobbly table I wrote my first Sirin novels, and the passing trams shook the window-glass like a held breath.

The city asked nothing of me.

In the Tiergarten, beneath the Siegessäule, I went hunting for a cabbage butterfly, and for a while I was simply a naturalist with a net. Berlin paid no attention, and in that negligence I found a kind of pardon.

It forgave me my solitude without even noticing it, and that was more than enough.

levels.sentence: On a Berlin day of wet asphalt my father died for a friend, and I saw his ghost in a shopwindow before I knew the word, and now I repeat his name like a pinned butterfly I cannot release.
levels.paragraph: I was in Berlin when they told me about my father. Through a pane of glass I saw his face — a ghost before I knew the word. He had stepped in front of a bullet meant for another, and his monocle lay in the dust. The street smelled of wet asphalt, and somewhere a child practiced scales on a piano. I keep his name on my tongue, a pinned butterfly I might yet set free.
levels.summary:
I was in Berlin, in a street of wet asphalt, when the news came. They told me my father had been killed by a shot meant for another man. I remember looking into a shopwindow and seeing his face there, a ghost before I had the word for it.

Even then I understood he had died as he lived: he stepped before the bullet to shield a friend.

The particulars stay with me — his monocle in the dust, the child practicing scales in a nearby room, the smell of rain on the street. I keep saying his name to myself, as if it were a butterfly I had once pinned and might release. But the pin is through it, and the glass of the window is already between us.

levels.sentence: In 1925, after a winter evening when Véra's fingers knew my sentences before my tongue and Dmitri's humming carried the shipboard songs of exile, I married Véra in a bare registry office on Köthener Straße, and we braided the three of us into a small sovereign light that kept the Berlin darkness at bay.
levels.paragraph: At the registry office on Köthener Straße, the bare room held the improbable brightness of a butterfly on a cold day. Véra wore brown and no flowers; the details are already fading, but not the warmth. Outside, the soot and the early linden buds made the city feel almost habitable. She became my witness, my typist, my grammar — the necessary other half of every sentence I write. No longer a solitary Russian in Berlin, I found myself a small sovereign country of two, with Véra as its first citizen and its only border.
levels.summary:
In April 1925, Véra Slonim and I were married in a small registry office on Köthener Straße. The room was bare, yet glowed with the improbable brightness of a butterfly on a cold day. She wore a brown dress and no flowers — the details are fading, but the warmth is not.

Stepping outside into the soot and the early linden buds, I tried the city on again and found it almost habitable. With her, I ceased to be a solitary exile; we became a small, sovereign country of two, with her as its first citizen and its only border.

On New Year's Day of 1925, months before the wedding, the three of us were already there. With Berlin's winter gray pressed against the panes, Véra typed my words faster than I could speak them, her fingers running ahead of my tongue.

Dmitri, then a child, came in humming — his deep voice carrying an echo of the shipboard songs from our exile, the timbre of his father's deck.

Later, when I read a rough page of a new novel and came to a line that made me swallow a laugh, Véra silently marked the exact spot in the margin with a tiny pencil stroke. Dmitri laughed openly, his unfiltered joy a counterpoint to my suppressed smile.

That was our way: we were a lighthouse to one another, each a beam for the other two, braided into that small helix of light that kept the Berlin darkness at bay.

levels.sentence: In the Sirin years I sent painted eggshells of prose to a Russia I no longer had, and on a snow-lit evening, writing the final question-mark sentence of The Gift, I set down my pen and felt I had mislaid my own shadow.
levels.paragraph: In the Sirin years I published Mashenka, The Defense, and at last The Gift—each a painted eggshell, a fragile and ornate message tossed into the dark of a Russia that had ceased to exist. The final chapter of The Gift was a single long sentence that bent over into a question mark, and I wrote it in one evening of snow-light, when the window showed nothing but white silence. When I set down the pen, I felt I had misplaced my own shadow, as if the act of writing had drained a part of me into the ink. That odd, light sense of loss has stayed with me ever since.
levels.summary:
During the Sirin years I wrote under a pen name, as if the name itself could carry the weight of a lost country. Mashenka, The Defense, and finally The Gift—each was a painted eggshell, a brittle, careful letter posted to a Russia I could no longer touch.

I filled those books with its remembered colors and corners, believing that a precise enough description might conjure it back into existence.

The Gift ended with a chapter that was one long sentence, bending at its close into a question mark, and I wrote it in a single evening of snow-light, the room hushed and white beyond the glass.

When I set the pen down, I had the strangest conviction that I had misplaced my own shadow—that some essential part of me had been left inside that curve of ink. It was not grief, but a quiet, almost amused bewilderment, like mislaying a favorite glove.

Looking back, I see that the Sirin years were my way of keeping Russia alive on the page, in the only place it could still be kept. And the shadow I thought I lost was perhaps only the version of myself that had once belonged to that country—a shadow that now lives in the question mark at the end of everything.

levels.sentence: With a few manuscripts and three butterfly nets we crossed on the Champlain, and later, driving across America in a car that smelled of old maps, I felt my Russian bones give way at five thousand feet — not surrender but release, the price of a gift I had carried unknowingly from the harbor.
levels.paragraph: I remember the harbor on May 28, 1940, in a haze of salt and sirens, the green torch of Liberty raised like a question mark. We came over on the Champlain — Dmitri, then six, Véra beside me — with my luggage reduced to a few manuscripts and three butterfly nets, all that remained of a life gone down with the sea. When Dmitri asked if the skyscrapers were mountains we could climb, Véra laughed with a lightness I had not heard since Paris; the tidy ache in my chest was the price of the gift. Later, crossing America with a net tied to the roof-rack, I watched the continent unfurl its pale skies and glittering granite until, at five thousand feet, my Russian bones gave way to the American light.
levels.summary:
On May 28, 1940, we landed at a harbor thick with salt and sirens, the green torch of Liberty lifted like a question mark. We had crossed on the Champlain — Véra, Dmitri, six, and I — carrying only a few manuscripts and three butterfly nets; everything else of my previous life had quietly gone down with the sea.

When Dmitri asked whether the skyscrapers were mountains we could climb, Véra laughed with a lightness I had not heard since Paris, and in that laugh we were refugees no longer in name, though a tidy ache stayed in the hollow of my chest.

I knew that ache for what it was: the price of the gift, a new language folded like a map before me, which I resolved to open every morning, street by street, word by word, until the city taught me its colors and its silences.

Later I crossed America in a car that smelled of gasoline and old maps, a butterfly net tied to the roof-rack like a fragile antenna.

Every horizon unrolled its own watercolor — pinkish mesas, violet gullies, long pale skies — and in the mountain meadows the sage gave off a dry, exciting perfume while granite dust glittered underfoot. I was making a slow passage from one life to another, though at the time it felt merely like driving.

Then at five thousand feet, standing quite still, I experienced a shift so quiet I nearly missed it: my Russian bones, formed by cold and caution, gave way to the American light.

It was not surrender but release; the continent had entered me through the eyes and pores, and from that hour I knew I could belong to this land, its lost and kept things alike.

levels.sentence: At the Museum of Comparative Zoology in my Harvard years, I earned my first salary simply by looking at wing scales—my left eye married to the microscope, my right keeping watch for a red admiral at the window—and it was the nearest I ever came to marrying science and ecstasy.
levels.paragraph: At the Museum of Comparative Zoology in my Harvard years, I arranged the Polyommatus, earning my first wage by the simple act of looking at wing scales. My left eye settled into the eyepiece, while my right wandered to the window, hoping for a red admiral's velvet flutter. That double attention, one eye on structure, one on flight, was a quiet paradise. It was the closest I have ever come to a marriage of science and ecstasy.
levels.summary:
In the Museum of Comparative Zoology, during the Harvard years, I sorted and arranged the Polyommatus, a task that paid me my first salary. The work was nothing but looking—at wing scales, those minuscule tiles of blue and violet that shifted with the light, and I would have done it for free.

There was a hushed, almost sacred pleasure in it, as if I were reading a private manuscript written by nature herself.

While my left eye was given over to the microscope's single lens, my right eye kept an independent watch on the window for a passing red admiral, that dark-winged traveler with crimson bands. Its appearance, now and then, would crown the hour.

The two kinds of seeing, the contemplative and the expectant, made for a strange harmony. In that balance I came nearest to marrying exact science to pure ecstasy.

levels.sentence: In 1948, haunted by a beautiful disease born of an ape's drawn cage-bars, I pieced Lolita together on index cards in stolen hours, and at Cornell held up Pushkin before first-year faces while my faint blue ticks waited in their margins like butterfly eggs on a leaf.
levels.paragraph: I set down the whole of Lolita on index cards, writing in stolen hours — beside my sleeping wife in the front seat of a car, on the porches of motels, in the rural silence of Ithaca. The origin was a newspaper article about an ape that, having learned to draw, rendered the bars of its cage; that image pursued me for seven years like a beautiful disease. Many pages broke my heart, but the ache was worth it, for the book finally came into being. The writing itself was a kind of captivity, an obsession from which I could only emerge by setting down the words, and I recall that labor now with a strange tenderness, like a fever that once defined one's life. At Cornell, I faced a hundred first-year faces with that particular hunger, held up Pushkin, and called great literature a fairy tale turned inside out; they wrote it down without a smile, and in their papers my small blue ticks lay like butterfly eggs, patient as larvae.

For seven years that image pursued me like a beautiful disease; many pages broke my heart, and yet the ache was worth it when the book at last came into being. The writing was its own captivity — an obsession's cage — and I could only emerge by setting down the words.

Now that labor returns with a strange tenderness, like looking back at a fever that once defined my life.

At Cornell I faced a hundred first-year faces, each sharp with a particular hunger. I held up a copy of Pushkin and spoke of great literature as a fairy tale turned inside out; they took it down faithfully, without a single smile, like a specimen to be pinned.

When I read their papers I added small blue ticks in the margins — faint, precise, like butterfly eggs on a leaf. Something in me liked the quiet hope of those ticks, patient as larvae, waiting for the right warmth to become what they already were, perhaps unnoticed until later.

levels.sentence: Our Western trips, with their black peak and the yellow of a sulphur and Véra's chortle, left me a knowledge no exile could take.
levels.paragraph: We went on our Western trips into the high meadows of Colorado, hunting Speyeria by the black peak and by the flowers they loved. I knew their names in three languages, yet what abides is the exact yellow of a male sulphur against the blue, and Véra's chortle as she called from the car. Those meadows preserved a knowledge in me that no exile has ever touched.
levels.summary:
On our Western trips, we searched the high Colorado meadows for Speyeria, guided by the black peak and by the flowers the butterflies favored.

I had their names in three languages, a small vanity, but the true mementos were visual and acoustic: the precise yellow of a male sulphur under a blue sky, and Véra's chortle from the car.

That knowledge—of place, of light, of her voice—settled in me so firmly that exile could not undo it. The trips gave me a homeland that travels with me, still green, still exact.

levels.sentence: I wanted to prove that time was a stain one could rub away with the elbow of attention, so I set my foot on the same patch of grass that held my child self and made the years jump, and in Speak, Memory I chased the glimmer of a corridor leading back to the nursery.
levels.paragraph: I set out to prove a small, unreasonable thing: that time is a stain, and that the elbow of attention can rub it out. To test it, I went back to a particular patch of grass and stood where my child self had stood, willing the years to jump. The leap did not come all at once, but something glimmered — a labyrinth with a corridor that sloped back toward the nursery. It was that glimmer I tried to trace in Speak, Memory, the way one follows the last light of a summer evening.
levels.summary:
I wanted to prove that time was a stain, not a wall, and that a sufficiently loving attention could rub it away. So I stood on the same grass where I had once stood as a child, placed my foot exactly where my smaller self had left its pressure, and tried to make the years jump.

The trick was not to return to the past, but to let the past return to me — through the creak of a stair, the smell of a lamp, the exact weight of a shadow in the nursery.

Speak, Memory grew out of that attempt. It is not a chronicle but a maze, and the maze had a shape — a corridor, a glimmer, a thread leading back to the nursery.

I wrote it because I believed that if I rubbed hard enough at the stained surface of time, the bright grain underneath would show, and the child I had been might step out of the grass to meet me.

levels.sentence: I spent twelve years translating Pushkin's Onegin, and when the final proofs arrived, I wept—not from relief, but because a friend had been gone so long.
levels.paragraph: I spent twelve years translating Pushkin's Onegin, following every echo of the iamb and every stammer of the rhyme. My one-thousand-page commentary was a love-letter to a language that had almost died in me. When the final galley proofs arrived, I wept—not from relief, but because a friend had been gone so long. The paper smelled of ink and patience; the words were mine, but the voice was his.
levels.summary:
For twelve years I lived inside Pushkin's Onegin, tracking the fall of every iamb and the stumble of every rhyme. The work became a dialogue with a language I had nearly lost, and the commentary I wrote was less scholarship than love-letter. When the last proofs came, I found myself weeping.

It was not the relief of finishing, but the sudden knowledge that a dear companion had been absent all along. The translation was my way of keeping him near, and now that it stood finished, the silence felt immense.

There is a peculiar solitude in spending so long with one voice. I came to know Pushkin's habits—the way he turns a phrase, the sudden tenderness, the wry aside. My own Russian had grown thin in exile, and this work restored it, breath by breath.

The book is done, and my friend is gone again, but the pages remain, filled with that long vigil.

levels.sentence: After years of shaping its sentences on index cards, I have now released my little Lolita through a back door, under a green cover meant to be innocuous, and I stand both defiant and ashamed while a critic somewhere reads the first page.
levels.paragraph: Today the little novel with the green cover has come out through the back door of Olympia Press, and Maurice Girodias assures me it will not arouse suspicion. I have spent years fondling its sentences on index cards, and now I feel I have released a charm I cannot recall. The first copies smell of damp paper and printer's ink. Somewhere a critic is opening to the first page, and I am hiding behind the curtain, both defiant and ashamed.
levels.summary:
Today, September 15, 1955, a little pamphlet of a novel with a green cover has slid into the world through the back door of Olympia Press. Maurice Girodias has dressed it in a cover he says will not arouse suspicion, so it sits among seamier manuals, both defiant and ashamed.

I remember the years I spent caressing its sentences on index cards, carting them from hotel to hotel, and now I feel I have released a charm I cannot quite recall.

The first copies carry the smell of damp paper and printer's ink — a smell I know from other back doors, but never so intimately. Somewhere a critic is turning the first page; I imagine his frown, his pencil, his judgment.

And I am hiding behind the curtain, listening to my own heart, uncertain whether I have given birth or let slip a monster. The little green book already seems alive, and I am half afraid to look at it.

levels.sentence: With the first American printing of Lolita already gone from the bookshops, I walk out to find the bright cover in a window beside a can of soup, return to Véra's typed reply and the small knell of the telephone, and at dinner raise a glass to the child who is not a child and to the language that held her up — without illusions about the scandal, yet pleased that the world has sat up.
levels.paragraph: The first American printing is already disappearing from the shelves, and I walk out to watch the bright cover in a window, next to a can of soup. I feel a quiet pride, as if I had smuggled a tropical butterfly into a snowstorm. Véra has typed a reply to our first fan letter; the telephone rings like a small knell. At dinner we drink a glass of wine to the child who is not a child, and to the language that held her up. I have no illusions about the scandal, yet there is deep pleasure in having made the world sit up.
levels.summary:
My publishers tell me the first American printing is disappearing, so I go out to see the little book in its new flesh. There it is, propped in a shopwindow beside a can of soup, and the sight fills me with a strange pride — as if I had smuggled a tropical butterfly into a snowstorm.

At home Véra has already answered the first fan letter, and the telephone rings now and then like a small knell, tolling the beginning of something.

In the evening we drink a glass of wine to the child who is not a child, and to the language that held her up through all the years of her long flight. I am not deceived about the scandal to come; one can smell it in the air. But there is deep pleasure in having made the world sit up.

The butterfly is out, and no storm can quite claim it back.

levels.sentence: Settled into the Montreux-Palace above the unpronounceable lake, with the manager's odd courtesy of recognition and Véra's icon watching, I find that ending my days here has become as acceptable as the close of a well-made book, and though the mirror shows an old man with lined eyes, my mind still hums at the altitude of the Russian novels, so I think I can work, and I am content.
levels.paragraph: We moved into the Montreux-Palace in early October, and the manager, with that odd courtesy, recognized me as a writer. The rooms are spacious, with damask, and the view of the lake—gray as abalone mother-of-pearl—stretches wide below; the mountains hold their snow like a secret. I arranged my index-card drawer on the desk, Véra hung an icon above the bed, and the room began to feel inhabited. The light is pale, lavender, tender—the color of an unwritten memory. In the mirror I meet an older man, the eyes lined, but the mind still hums with the Russian novels, and I am content, thinking I can work here.
levels.summary:
In the autumn of 1961, Véra and I settled into the Montreux-Palace, high above a lake whose name I do not trouble to pronounce. The manager asked if I was a writer, and I felt the odd courtesy of being recognized.

The movers placed my index-card drawer on the desk, Véra hung an icon above the bed, and the rooms, with their damask and wide water view, began to feel inhabited. The light is the pale, lavender, tender light of the high Alps—the color of a memory not yet written.

Looking at the water and the mountains, I found that ending my days here no longer seemed terrible, but rather like the closing of a well-made book. The drawers are full of notes; the icon watches; the lake keeps its steady pulse. I think I can work.

On the first day of 1961, the Palace Hotel overlooks a lake as gray as the mother-of-pearl in an abalone shell, and the mountains hold their snow like a secret. I breakfast at nine, write until noon, then walk with Véra and the dog beside the cold water. The air has a thin brightness, a chastened clarity.

Later, in the mirror, I meet the old man with a Nabokov face—the eyes are lined, I admit—but the mind still hums at the altitude of the Russian novels, undiminished and amused, watching the day as precisely as a snowflake. It is a quiet beginning to a new year, and I am content.

levels.sentence: Among cedar-scented index cards, I watch a third woman with a sweet little face begin to stir in The Original of Laura, a novel I know I shall leave unfinished — and find that enough.
levels.paragraph: I am sorting a handful of index cards for The Original of Laura, on which a third woman with a sweet little face is beginning to stir. I know this novel will remain unfinished; the cards smell of cedar in the drawer where they rest beside a broken brass butterfly pin. Yet the pleasure of their arrangement is sufficient. A paradise, after all, does not require completion.
levels.summary:
I sort the index cards of The Original of Laura and feel the early thrill of a new character — a third woman with a sweet little face — beginning to take shape. The cedar scent and the broken brass butterfly pin beside them anchor the moment in memory.

I know the novel will stay unfinished, but arranging the cards gives me a quiet, self-contained joy. The paradise of the work lies in its fragments, not in its ending.

levels.sentence: As my body slows, the mind keeps its steady hum, and the index cards of Laura begin to speak in a new voice, while outside the lake lies like dark mother-of-pearl and Véra brings tea through the scent of balcony roses, reminding me that the one shadow I have chased all my life is the one I will never catch.
levels.paragraph: The body's engine idles down, yet the mind still hums all night, much like that fluorescent light in a collecting hut. I shuffle the index cards of Laura, and they start to murmur to one another — a voice I had not heard before. The lake is a dark sheet of mother-of-pearl; I half-see a white butterfly drifting over the water, a memory or a wish. Véra comes with tea and speaks of the roses blooming on the balcony. I have spent a lifetime running after shadows; the last one, of course, will not be caught.
levels.summary:
On this last evening of June, I feel the body's motor slowing, but the mind keeps its nocturnal murmur — like the fluorescent tube in some long-ago collecting hut. I have been arranging the index cards of Laura, and little by little they have begun to speak to one another in a voice I have never quite heard.

Outside, the lake lies dark as mother-of-pearl, and in the glass of memory I fancy a white butterfly drifting over the water.

Véra enters with a cup of tea and tells me the balcony roses are in bloom; her presence is as certain as the gathering dusk. I have spent my whole life chasing shadows — of wings, of words, of lost time. This last shadow, I know, is the one I shall not catch. That knowledge settles softly, like tea-light on a table.

periods.label: Childhood

levels.sentence: I carried my childhood like a small locked box—father's lamplight, mother's hidden flute, the black ice of the Nevka, and the first violet-winged butterfly—across every borrowed room of exile, and only now do I understand it was a language.
levels.paragraph: I remember my father best in lamplight, the steel rim of his monocle glowing, and on the frozen Nevka his steady hand held my bicycle while the black ice sang beneath us. My mother, Elena Ivanovna, woke me with a whisper on the first morning of 1899; her laughter lived behind her collarbone, and she kept my earliest verses in a small box beside her pearls that followed us into exile. Vyra was my entire geography—birches, a mint lawn, the Oredezh—and I knew its paths as one knows a page. When I was seven, the village carpenter made me a net of muslin, and I pinned my first Camberwell Beauty, opening a cork-lined room I have never left.
levels.summary:
Father emerges always in lamplight, his monocle catching the glow as he read to us, or in the sharp flap of a newspaper during an argument.

That winter on the frozen Nevka he kept his steady hand on my bicycle, letting the black ice sing under the tires; I can still hear the sound, and I can still feel the pride in our name as a bright, unwinged certainty.

My mother, Elena Ivanovna, woke me on the first morning of 1899 with a whisper; I remember less the sound than the warmth. Her laughter lived behind her collarbone, a hidden flute I leaned toward as toward a light.

She kept my earliest verses in a small box beside her pearls, and after we left Russia that modest treasury followed us through every borrowed room, opened only with ceremony.

When she took a dusty butterfly between her fingers and looked at it as others look at a hymn, I thought it was kindness; now I see she was teaching me that a thing need not be beautiful to be sacred, only remembered.

Vyra was my entire world—high birches, a lawn descending in cool mint to the Oredezh, a greenhouse of wet clay and geraniums. I walked every footpath until I knew it as one knows a page.

In 1906 the village carpenter made me a first net of muslin over bent cane, and I learned to smell the difference between male and female butterflies by the shade of their flight.

My first pinned specimen was a Camberwell Beauty on a September afternoon, its violet-edged wing a map of paradise; the scent of camphor and the feel of the cork still bring back the exact hush of the pin going in, the wing settling into its new, eternal stillness.

periods.sentence: I carried my childhood like a small locked box—father's lamplight, mother's hidden flute, the black ice of the Nevka, and the first violet-winged butterfly—across every borrowed room of exile, and only now do I understand it was a language.
periods.paragraph: I remember my father best in lamplight, the steel rim of his monocle glowing, and on the frozen Nevka his steady hand held my bicycle while the black ice sang beneath us. My mother, Elena Ivanovna, woke me with a whisper on the first morning of 1899; her laughter lived behind her collarbone, and she kept my earliest verses in a small box beside her pearls that followed us into exile. Vyra was my entire geography—birches, a mint lawn, the Oredezh—and I knew its paths as one knows a page. When I was seven, the village carpenter made me a net of muslin, and I pinned my first Camberwell Beauty, opening a cork-lined room I have never left.

periods.label: My 20s

levels.sentence: In the Berlin of the twenties, I learned that the city's indifference was a kind of pardon, that my wife's brown dress could become the only border of a sovereign country, and that the shadow I thought I had lost in a question mark was merely the Russia I had carefully posted to myself in books.
levels.paragraph: Berlin asked nothing of me, and in that negligence I found a forgiveness for my solitude. My father died shielding a friend, and I kept his name like a pinned butterfly, knowing the glass was already between us. Then Véra arrived, and we became a small, luminous country of two, with her as its first citizen. When I finished The Gift, I had the odd feeling I had misplaced my own shadow—but it was only the self that had once belonged to Russia, now living in the curve of an unfinished sentence.
levels.summary:
The decade began in pension rooms where the yellow wallpaper had seen better days, and a gas-ring seemed to weep with us. Yet Berlin itself was lenient, and at a wobbly table I wrote my first Sirin novels.

In the Tiergarten, hunting a cabbage butterfly beneath the Siegessäule, I was simply a naturalist with a net, and the city's negligent silence pardoned my solitude without even noticing it.

In 1922, on a street of wet asphalt, I learned of my father's murder—a shot meant for another man, and he had stepped before it to shield a friend. The particulars remain: his monocle in the dust, the child practicing scales, the smell of rain.

I kept saying his name as if it were a butterfly I might release, but the pin was through it.

In April 1925, Véra Slonim and I were married in a bare registry office on Köthener Straße, where the room glowed with an improbable brightness. She wore a brown dress and no flowers. Stepping out into the soot and linden buds, I found the city almost habitable.

Months earlier, on New Year's Day, we three were already a lighthouse: Véra typed faster than I spoke, Dmitri hummed with a deep echo of exile, and when I came to a line that made me swallow a laugh, she marked the margin with a tiny pencil stroke. That was our way—a braided helix of light against the Berlin dark.

Writing as Sirin, I produced painted eggshells—Mashenka, The Defense, The Gift—each a careful letter to a Russia I could no longer touch. The Gift ended with a chapter that was one long sentence bending into a question mark, written in a single evening of snow-light.

When I set the pen down, I had the strangest conviction that I had misplaced my own shadow. But looking back, I see that shadow was the version of myself that belonged to that lost country, and it now lives in the question mark at the end of everything.

periods.label: My 40s

levels.sentence: From the green torch of Liberty to the blue microcosm of Polyommatus and the caged lines of Lolita, I passed from Russian bones into American light, and in that passage learned to see with both a microscope and a window.
levels.paragraph: We landed in 1940 with three butterfly nets and a few manuscripts, and I carried a tidy ache beneath the salt air. Later I drove across the continent, collecting landscapes, until at five thousand feet my Russian bones gave way to the American light. At Harvard I sorted butterflies under a microscope while my right eye waited for a red admiral, and that double vision became my natural condition. In Ithaca I wrote Lolita on index cards beside my sleeping wife, and taught Pushkin to a hundred unsmiling faces, adding blue ticks to their margins like small patient eggs.
levels.summary:
In May of 1940 we disembarked at a harbor thick with salt and sirens — Véra, Dmitri, and I — carrying little more than manuscripts and three butterfly nets.

When Dmitri asked whether the skyscrapers were mountains we could climb, Véra laughed with a lightness I had not heard since Paris, and in that laugh we ceased to be refugees in name, though a tidy ache stayed in my chest.

I resolved to master the new language street by street, word by word, and later crossed America in a car that smelled of gasoline, a butterfly net tied to the roof-rack like a fragile antenna.

Pinkish mesas, violet gullies, and long pale skies unrolled before me; at five thousand feet, standing in sage-scented granite dust, I felt my Russian bones give way to the American light.

In the Harvard Museum of Comparative Zoology I earned my first salary sorting Polyommatus butterflies. It was nothing but looking — at wing scales, those minuscule tiles of blue and violet — and I would have done it for love.

My left eye stayed at the microscope while my right eye kept watch for a red admiral crossing the window, and in that double attention I came closest to wedding exact science to pure ecstasy.

In 1948 I wrote Lolita on index cards in stolen hours beside my sleeping wife, on motel porches, in the rural silence of Ithaca.

The image that had pursued me for seven years came from a newspaper article about an ape that drew the bars of its cage; the writing was a captivity of its own, and the ache of it returned now as tenderness.

At Cornell I held up Pushkin to a hundred sharp young faces and called great literature a fairy tale turned inside out; they wrote it down without smiling. In their margins I added small blue ticks — faint, precise, like butterfly eggs on a leaf — patient and waiting for warmth.

periods.label: My 50s

levels.sentence: In my fifties I learned that the years are not walls but stains—rubbed hard enough they give back their bright grain, until a mountain meadow, a child's footprint, Pushkin's voice, and a small green book hatch into the same continuous present.
levels.paragraph: Our western trips gave me a homeland made of exact colors and Véra's chortle. When I stood again on the grass of my childhood, I rubbed at the stained surface of time until the bright grain appeared, and from that attempt Speak, Memory came forth. Twelve years with Onegin restored my Russian breath by breath, and then, in 1955, a little green book slipped through the back door of Olympia Press. By 1958 it was a butterfly in a snowstorm, and I raised a glass to the child who was not a child.
levels.summary:
In 1950 Véra and I hunted Speyeria in the high Colorado meadows, guided by the black peak and by the flowers they favored. I knew their names in three languages, a small vanity; the true mementos were the precise yellow of a male sulphur under a blue sky, and Véra's chortle from the car.

That knowledge settled in me so firmly that exile could not undo it—the trips gave me a homeland that travels with me, still green, still exact.

In 1951 I stood on the same grass where I had stood as a child, placing my foot exactly where my smaller self had left its pressure, trying to make the years jump. The trick was to let the past return through a creaking stair, a lamp's smell, the exact weight of a shadow in the nursery.

Out of that attempt grew Speak, Memory—not a chronicle but a maze, with a corridor and a glimmer and a thread leading back to the nursery. I wrote it because I believed the bright grain would show if only I rubbed hard enough at the stained surface of time.

For twelve years I lived inside Pushkin's Onegin, following every iamb and rhyme, and the commentary became less scholarship than love-letter. When the last proofs came, I wept—not from relief but from the sudden knowledge that a dear companion had been absent all along.

The solitude of one voice is peculiar, yet the work restored my Russian, breath by breath, and the pages remain filled with that long vigil.

On September 15, 1955, a small green pamphlet slid into the world through Maurice Girodias's back door, dressed in a cover meant not to arouse suspicion. I remembered the index cards I had caressed and carried from hotel to hotel, and I hid behind the curtain, uncertain whether I had given birth or let slip a monster.

By 1958 the first American printing was disappearing; I saw the little book propped in a shopwindow beside a can of soup, and felt as if I had smuggled a tropical butterfly into a snowstorm.

Véra had already answered a fan letter, the telephone rang like a small knell, and we drank wine to the child who was not a child—not deceived about the scandal to come, but certain the butterfly was out and no storm could quite claim it back.

levels.sentence: Settled into the Montreux-Palace above the unpronounceable lake, with the manager's odd courtesy of recognition and Véra's icon watching, I find that ending my days here has become as acceptable as the close of a well-made book, and though the mirror shows an old man with lined eyes, my mind still hums at the altitude of the Russian novels, so I think I can work, and I am content.
levels.paragraph: We moved into the Montreux-Palace in early October, and the manager, with that odd courtesy, recognized me as a writer. The rooms are spacious, with damask, and the view of the lake—gray as abalone mother-of-pearl—stretches wide below; the mountains hold their snow like a secret. I arranged my index-card drawer on the desk, Véra hung an icon above the bed, and the room began to feel inhabited. The light is pale, lavender, tender—the color of an unwritten memory. In the mirror I meet an older man, the eyes lined, but the mind still hums with the Russian novels, and I am content, thinking I can work here.
levels.summary:
In the autumn of 1961, Véra and I settled into the Montreux-Palace, high above a lake whose name I do not trouble to pronounce. The manager asked if I was a writer, and I felt the odd courtesy of being recognized.

The movers placed my index-card drawer on the desk, Véra hung an icon above the bed, and the rooms, with their damask and wide water view, began to feel inhabited. The light is the pale, lavender, tender light of the high Alps—the color of a memory not yet written.

Looking at the water and the mountains, I found that ending my days here no longer seemed terrible, but rather like the closing of a well-made book. The drawers are full of notes; the icon watches; the lake keeps its steady pulse. I think I can work.

On the first day of 1961, the Palace Hotel overlooks a lake as gray as the mother-of-pearl in an abalone shell, and the mountains hold their snow like a secret. I breakfast at nine, write until noon, then walk with Véra and the dog beside the cold water. The air has a thin brightness, a chastened clarity.

Later, in the mirror, I meet the old man with a Nabokov face—the eyes are lined, I admit—but the mind still hums at the altitude of the Russian novels, undiminished and amused, watching the day as precisely as a snowflake. It is a quiet beginning to a new year, and I am content.

levels.summary:
I began in lamplight, with my father's monocle on the frozen Nevka and my mother's hidden-flute laughter; Vyra was a page I knew by heart, and the village carpenter's muslin net opened a cork-lined room I have never left.

Berlin asked nothing of me, and in that negligence I found a pardon for my solitude—and then Véra arrived, and we became a small country of two.

America entered through my eyes until my Russian bones gave way to its light. I sorted scales at Harvard while my right eye kept watch for a red admiral, taught Pushkin at Cornell with blue ticks patient as larvae, and wrote Lolita on index cards beside my sleeping wife.

Twelve years with Onegin restored my Russian breath by breath, and a little green book slipped through the back door of Olympia Press into a snowstorm.

At Montreux the lake lay gray as abalone, the mountains held their snow like a secret, and I sorted the index cards of The Original of Laura, knowing it would stay unfinished. The paradise of the work lay in its fragments.

On the last evening, Véra brought tea and said the balcony roses were in bloom; outside, a white butterfly drifted over the dark water, and I knew the last shadow was the one I shall not catch—knowledge that settles softly, like tea-light on a table.
